purpose: Append-only notebook for the COW synthesis loop. The loop runs unattended, so anything a human would want to know afterwards goes here instead of stopping the run: fidelity judgements worth a second opinion, tool flags the writer overrode, defects found in the source, and chapters the driver rejected.
how: Never hand-edit. Append with: python3 scripts/synthesis-note.py --book <book> --chapter <ch> --kind <kind> --note '<text>' [--verses 3,7]. Review with: python3 scripts/synthesis-note.py --list [--kind ...] [--since YYYY-MM-DD].

kinds.fidelity: why a verse was graded B, or an A that felt borderline
kinds.disagreement: a STRETCH / ENTITIES / UNSOURCED flag the writer judged a false positive, and why
kinds.source-defect: scrape residue, a misplaced witness block, an out-of-range verse key
kinds.rejected: written by the driver when a chapter fails verification and is reverted
kinds.observation: anything else the next reader should know

Corpus-wide scan: 575 verses across 387 chapters have this shape - raw blob over 200 words, usable material under 200 once the noise block is dropped. Worst offenders psalms 78, ezekiel 23, numbers 31 (6 verses each). The two rules genuinely conflict: 'skip noise silently' tells the writer to ignore the residue, while the thin exemption measures the source WITH it. The fix is one line in validate-synthesis.py source_words(): measure after stripping the same noise the writer is required to ignore. That LOOSENS the exemption, so no committed chapter can break. Not changed unilaterally - the loop doc records the floor and the exemption as owner decisions.

Numbers 7 is also the largest unit in the corpus at 89 verses, 72 of them the repeated tribal offering with 12-21 words of source each. Even unblocked it is the chapter most likely to produce templated filler, and the anti-templating rule (Job 5 precedent) bites hardest here. Worth handling deliberately rather than as a routine queue item.

Driver/environment bug worth fixing: in the scheduled CCR container the repo is checked out with a DETACHED HEAD. synthesis-loop.py push_chapter runs 'git push -u origin master', which in that state pushes the stale local branch 'master' rather than HEAD, so every attempt is rejected as non-fast-forward and finish reports 'push rejected four times' (exit 4) even though the commit is sound and 'git push origin HEAD:master' would fast-forward. Worked around by hand this run: git checkout -B master <commit>, git reset --mixed origin/master, re-run finish --push. Suggested fix: push HEAD:master, or refuse to start when HEAD is detached.

The 28-30 entry self-graded B. Henry lists the deaths that would have disproved Moses (plague, fire from heaven, the sword) and separately calls the earth opening 'a punishment without precedent'; the entry joins those into the inference that fire from heaven was named precisely because it had precedent and this appeal required something with none. The claim is sound and nothing is put into Henry's mouth, but the connective is the summary's, not his. Every other entry graded A.

Two live disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Whether Korah died in the chasm or in the fire: Ellicott and Wesley both argue for the fire, from the sons who did not die, from Deuteronomy 11:6 naming only Dathan and Abiram, and from Psalm 106:17-18 dividing the two punishments — against the plain reading of v.32 and the later summary that names Korah with the other two. (2) What metal the priests' own censers were: Gill says silver (gold only on the day of atonement) and reads the specification of brass here as marking Korah's vessels off from Aaron's; Ellicott finds no sufficient authority for silver and points to Exodus 38:3. Also recorded: Calvin holds the censers were preserved as accursed under a ban, against the commoner view that a thing once put to holy use may not return to common service.

Ellicott's note on v.40 cites the Jude parallel as 'Numbers 16:11' — a misprint for Jude 11, since the sentence is about the apostle warning Christians by this example. Written as 'the epistle of Jude' with no numeric ref rather than reproducing the bad citation.

Calvin reckons the company destroyed with Korah at 'about three hundred' where the text says two hundred and fifty; the figure is his, and the entry attributes it to him rather than correcting it silently or repeating it as fact.

Three live disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Whether the seclusion was hygienic or purely ceremonial: Ellicott states flatly that leprosy was not contagious and argues it from the emptying of the house before inspection (v.36), while Wesley has the man kept out of his tent lest leprosy still lurking in him infect his family (v.8). (2) Whether house-leprosy was supernatural: Ellicott takes 'I put the plague' at face value as the immediate hand of God, Clarke answers that scripture often represents God as doing what in providence he only permits, and guesses animalcula. (3) What 'to teach' governs in v.57: Ellicott reads it as instruction against the time when the cases would have to be judged in the land, the ancient authorities and the Chaldee as instruction about which days a plague may be inspected on — Wesley's gloss, that the priest was tied to rules the people could discern as well as he could, sits with neither exactly.

The 36-38 entry self-graded B. The inference is his and the clause is faithful to it, but the formulation is the summary's. Every other entry graded A.

ENTITIES flag on the 23-26 entry judged a false positive: the source header reads 'TITUS BOST;', an abbreviation the prose expands to the standard form 'Titus of Bostra'. (1) Who pronounces sentence on the husbandmen (v.16): Theophylact has the Jews give the verdict first and then recoil with 'God forbid' once they catch the parable's drift, while Augustine divides the crowd, one part answering truly and another protesting. (2) What the two fates of v.18 are: Cyril distinguishes the ruin of their souls in taking offence from the ruin of the nation in the captivity, while Bede grades them by degree and leaves the believing sinner room for penitence. BLOCKER — this chapter cannot be written to contract as the source stands, and the next worker will hit the same wall. Two findings. (1) The catena is incomplete: source keys are 1-32, 36, 37, 42, 48-54; verses 33-35, 38-41 and 43-47 are absent entirely. (2) An identical 207-word Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block on the tribal princes' offerings of Numbers 7 ('This tribe being stationed on the right side of Judah, offered next through its representative...') is mechanically inserted at every SIXTH key — 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54. The conflict: verse 42 is isolated (41 and 43 are not source keys), so no pericope range can absorb it without covering verses absent from the source, which coverage_problems rejects; and declaring a range ANYWHERE in the chapter switches coverage enforcement on for the whole chapter, which then demands an entry for key 42 that cannot honestly be written. Three ways out, none of which an unattended run should choose alone: (a) write the chapter with NO declared range, which leaves coverage unenforced so keys 36 and 42 can simply be omitted as residue-only, on the 2 Chronicles 27 key-16 precedent — but then several tiny verses (v.21 has 23 usable words, v.29 has 36, v.16 and v.31 have 50) must each carry a 120-word thin entry, which is padding by contract at 3-5x; (b) drop keys 36 and 42 from the source file as scrape corruption, which makes the ranged solution legal and is the cleanest fix, but edits the data tree; (c) re-scrape the chapter, since 12 of 54 verses are missing anyway. Recommend (b) or (c), owner's call. Chapter size for whoever takes it after the fix: 42 keys, 19,991 source words.

Four disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over, and the first is the chapter's whole crux. (1) What the gift of tongues was (v.2): Ellicott argues at length that it was not languages at all — from the vocabulary (glossa never dialektos), from its never being used to preach to foreigners (the apostles did not understand Lycaonian), and from the description here of impassioned utterance expressing feeling rather than thought; Lightfoot and Clarke hold it was Hebrew, a dead language restored to the church and read there as in the synagogue. Ellicott and Calvin both note that the word 'unknown' is not in the Greek at all but was supplied by the seventeenth-century revisers, which quietly settles the question in favour of one theory wherever the AV is read. (2) What the mysteries of v.2 are: special revelations from God (Chrysostom) or dark and involved sayings of no profit (Calvin). (3) What the silence of v.34 covers: disputing and questioning on the synagogue model, leaving 1 Cor 11 and any extraordinary impulse untouched (Clarke, Wesley); public speaking generally, teaching being inconsistent with subjection, though Calvin allows a necessity may require it (Henry, Calvin); or Robertson, who declines to draw the line at all, sets Paul's plain meaning beside the daughters of Philip and the practice of his own day, and ends asking for patience rather than issuing a ruling. His refusal is recorded as a position in its own right, not flattened into one of the other two. (4) The textual variant at v.38, where Ellicott gives both readings equal weight.

Not attempted (worker context exhausted; nothing claimed). 40 verses, 75,582 source words — the largest unit offered in six picks, and unlike Joshua 15 or 19 it is dense doctrinal argument on marriage and celibacy with no register structure, so pericope grouping buys almost nothing and it needs near per-verse treatment. Budget it as a whole batch for a fresh worker, or more. WORTH THE MAINTAINER'S ATTENTION, measured rather than impressionistic: --worst-first systematically hands out chapters well above corpus size. Across all 1,189 cow chapters the median is 19,611 source words and the mean 27,059; the visible head of the worst-first repair queue has a median of 30,409 and a mean of 36,482, i.e. roughly 1.55x the corpus median. The cause is structural, not a bug — defect weight counts defective verses, and verse count correlates with source size, so the worst-first ordering is also a longest-first ordering. Two consequences. (1) A batch budget should be planned around ~30k source words per chapter, not the corpus median. (2) The tail is severe: 1 Corinthians 15 sits in the current window at 116,326 words and the corpus maximum is 150,785, while 37.6% of all chapters are 25k or larger. If workers are to keep clearing the queue rather than returning surveys, the scheduled prompt's 'up to 2 chapters' is the wrong unit for this end of the queue — one chapter, or an explicit size cap on the pick, would fit it better. My own six picks bear this out: 34.7k, 28.3k, 30.6k, 68.7k, 20.0k, 18.9k and now 75.6k.

Per-verse voice map was built BEFORE spans were chosen this time, and it drove the boundaries. Four genuine disagreements preserved: how wide the occasion for a thanksgiving offering runs (Jarchi, Aben Ezra and Ellicott confine it to notable deliverances, Gill extends it to the common mercies of life); what marks off the second class of peace offering (Ellicott's canon-law distinction between a vow binding the person and a freewill offering binding only the animal, against Calvin's reading that the vow meant here is simple rather than conditional, since a conditional vow paid would be thanksgiving); where the laws were given (Gill reads 'in mount Sinai' as by or near it, after the tabernacle stood, while Clarke has them given on the mount itself); and what 'the law of the consecrations' names (Ellicott the high priest's meat offering on entering office, Wesley the sacrifice at the consecration of the priests).

Clarke's block at v.8 carries a long Virgil quotation on sleeping upon sacrificial fleeces for dreams and an equally long note from Sir Walter Scott on the Highland togharm. Both are Clarke's own comparative material, so they were summarised rather than quoted, and kept — they are the most distinctive thing in the chapter's catena.

Entries 1 and 28 first graded B on repetition — low type-token ratio, not duplicated content (dupfrac 0.000 on both). The cause is the chapter's own vocabulary: offering, trespass, sin, peace, burnt, altar, priest, breast, shoulder recur unavoidably. Ellicott's blocks at v.37 and v.63 both run off into StudyLight page chrome: stylesheet rules, the full nav menu, a Cloudflare challenge snippet, a Stripe public key and the book_data array. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

A 63-verse boundary-and-town-list chapter, 30,562 source words, cut into sixteen entries. The voice map drove every span: Henry has blocks only at vv.1, 13, 20 and 28-35, Calvin only at 1, 13, 14, 18, 20 and 63, and both write section overviews rather than verse notes, so their material had to be used inside the entry covering the verse it is filed under. Two ghost attributions surfaced in the first check — Henry's Bethlehem remark and his note on the wilderness being thinly settled, both from the v.20 block, quoted in the 55-60 and 61-62 entries — and were rewritten out. The town lists (21-62) are mostly Gill and Keil at 200-300 words a verse; grouping them by the chapter's own district headings gives entries of workable length at expansion ratios of 0.15x to 0.36x.

Seven disagreements preserved rather than smoothed: whether the lot governed the division among families as well as tribes (Gill against Clarke and Wesley); what the river of Egypt is (Clarke calls it undecidable, Ellicott and Keil name the Wady el-Arish); where the valley of Hinnom lay (Jerome and Clarke east of Jerusalem, Reland and Keil south of Zion); when Caleb drove out the Anakim (Gill before Joshua's death, Calvin after); how Othniel was related to Caleb (Gill makes him a nephew to save the marriage from the incest law, Keil makes him Caleb's own younger brother and denies the law applies); why the town totals do not match the names (Simeon's transfer, the definition of a city, or corrupt compound names); why Gath and Ashkelon are unnamed (Gill's 'the three stand for the rest' against Keil's 'both lie inside the boundaries already given'); and how habitable the desert of Judah was (Keil's terrible desert against Gill's many cities and villages).

Clarke at v.58 reports that the Alexandrian and Vatican manuscripts of the Septuagint insert eleven further towns here, Ephratha (Bethlehem) among them, that Jerome knew them, and that Kennicott would restore them, explaining the loss as a transcriber's eye skipping between two occurrences of 'and their villages'. Keil independently records the same gap. This bears directly on Henry's remark at v.20 that Bethlehem's absence shows how little the town then was — if the eleven belong, the absence is a copyist's slip. The two are filed under different verses and so sit in different entries; the connection is drawn in the 55-60 entry without attributing Henry's remark there.

Two ENTITIES flags kept deliberately. 'Hadireh' is the source's 'Hadîreh' with the circumflex stripped. 'Onomasticon' expands the source's standing abbreviation 'Onom.' — same class as the Whitfield/Jerom spellings kept in earlier chapters. Four other flags were genuine and were fixed: 'Anakim' (Calvin spells it Enakim, Keil Anakites) reworded away; 'Masoretes' (source has Masorites) reworded to the received accentuation; 'Watchtower' was my translation of Keil's Alba Specula and was reverted to the Latin; 'Safieh' and 'Esdud' were misspellings of the source's Saphieh and of a mangled Esdûd.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears three times as scrape residue, none of it on Deuteronomy 2: at v.6 a fragment about rescuing ambassadors (2 Kings 6), at v.24 a passage about nomad tribes at the base of the Idumean mountain, at v.30 one about the scouts who did not join the mutinous murmuring. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 4, 24 and 26.
Ellicott's block at v.36 runs off into StudyLight page chrome — stylesheet rules, the nav menu and the site footer. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Ten entries over 37 verses, 14,593 source words. Henry writes only three blocks in this chapter (vv.1, 8 and 24) and each is a section overview covering many verses ahead, so his material had to be used inside the entry containing the verse it is filed under: his treatment of the ban on the Amorites sits under v.24 and therefore in the 24-25 entry, not in 33-35 where the slaughter is actually narrated. The first ghost check caught exactly that, plus Calvin quoted in 20-23 from his v.19 block and Clarke quoted in 17-19 from his v.20 block; all three were rewritten out. Worth noting that the ghost check does NOT catch the subtler error — attributing out-of-span material to a voice who happens to have some other block inside the span — which is how Ellicott's v.21 argument nearly stayed in the 17-19 entry.

Four disagreements preserved: how God could be said to have blessed the work of Israel's hands in a desert with no commerce (Calvin says their cattle increased and their labour yielded furniture and necessaries though they earned no wages; Ellicott sees nothing unreasonable in supposing ordinary trade, since they had skilled workmen); whether the Emim and Rephaim were giants (Gill and Wesley take the stature literally, Clarke insists Rephaim is a people's name and that fear and public report added the height); whether the embassy to Sihon preceded the command to attack (Calvin rearranges the verses into a pluperfect parenthesis, Keil and Henry keep the order and read the peace offer as leaving Sihon inexcusable); and what the hardening of Sihon's spirit means (Wesley's permissive 'suffered it to be hardened', Keil's judgment of hardening, and Ellicott's argument that God gave the strength and the same verb tells Joshua to be of good courage).

One ENTITIES flag fixed and two kept. 'Troglodytes' was corrected to the source's 'Troglodytae'. 'Jerome' is Gill's 'Jerom' in modern spelling, and 'Wady Mojib' is Ellicott's 'Wady Mojib' with the circumflexes stripped — both the same class of orthographic variant kept and noted in Exodus 30 and Joshua 15.

The three commentators who speak to the extermination of Sihon's people (Ellicott, Wesley, Keil) all press the same way: Ellicott insists the word will bear nothing less than devotion to destruction and that the narrative therefore asserts an extermination by express divine command, Wesley grounds it in the wickedness of the devoted nation, Keil describes the ban without qualification. None offers the softening reading. Henry alone, under v.24, enters the limiting principle — that the case was extraordinary and is not a precedent for war without quarter — which is recorded there rather than at 33-35 because that is where his block sits.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears three times as scrape residue, none of it on Exodus 26: at v.13 and v.31 fragments about the Shekinah cloud and the angel of God, at v.37 more of the same. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 7, 31 and 36.

Eight entries over 37 verses, 16,361 source words. The spans were re-cut once mid-draft: an entry keyed 22-25 had absorbed the bars (vv.26-29), whose commentary is filed under v.26 and later. The ghost check did NOT catch this, because Ellicott, Gill and Keil all have blocks inside 22-25 as well — the same blind spot recorded for Deuteronomy 2. Fixed by merging 22-25 and 26-30 into a single 22-30 entry, which also brought a thin pair up to a workable length. The lesson stands: the ghost check verifies that a cited voice is somewhere in the span, not that the material cited is.

Three disagreements preserved. On the thickness of the boards, Keil and Delitzsch reject both Josephus' four fingers and the cubit proposed by Rashi and Bahr, on the ground that a cubit-thick board could neither be cut from an acacia nor carried on a desert road. On the proportion of the two chambers, Keil gives ten cubits and twenty while Ellicott points out that 'under the taches', read strictly, makes them equal, and floats the Temple's half-size arrangement as a third possibility. On the word describing the door hanging, Ellicott builds his whole inwoven-versus-embroidered distinction on it, while Keil denies it means embroidery at all and holds for stripes or checks woven in mixed colours.

Two things in this chapter's catena are worth flagging for anyone working the tabernacle chapters. Calvin opens at v.1 by refusing the allegorical method outright — it was by no means God's intention to include mysteries in every hook and loop, and even if no part were without mystical meaning, which no one in his senses will admit, it is better to confess ignorance than indulge conjecture. He names the writer to the Hebrews as his model of restraint. And at v.36 Keil and Delitzsch publicly retract a reading they had printed in their own earlier Archaeologie, naming the Rabbins, Gesenius and Bahr as fellow-mistaken; the retraction unsettles Ellicott's distinction at v.1, so the two are recorded as a debate rather than harmonised.

Zero ENTITIES signals on the whole chapter — the first clean fidelity read-back in this run. The reason is probably that Exodus 26 has almost no place-names and no modern site identifications; the flags in Exodus 30, Joshua 15 and Deuteronomy 2 were nearly all transliterated toponyms or diacritics stripped from surveyors' spellings.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown is scrape residue at six verses in this chapter, none of it on Exodus 29: fragments about the wilderness murmuring, the quails and the tamarisk manna, and the faithful scouts. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 4, 15, 22, 26, 35 and 38.
Ellicott's block at v.46 runs off into StudyLight page chrome (footer, terms-of-use links). Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Eleven entries over 46 verses, 20,291 source words. One ghost attribution caught before validating: Keil and Delitzsch quoted in the 43-46 entry, where their block actually sits at v.42 and so falls in the 38-42 span. Replaced with Clarke and Ellicott, who do have blocks at 43-46. Six other entries first showed a substantive voice as excludable — Gill at v.1, Gill in 4-9, Wesley and Clarke in 15-18, Ellicott and Wesley in 26-34, Clarke in 38-42, Gill in 43-46 — in every case because I had simply not used a commentator who had real material there. All six were written in rather than declared excluded; excluded_voices is for residue, not for a writer's omissions.

One three-way disagreement preserved, on 'whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy'. Calvin reads it of the offerings, the altar sanctifying the victims laid on it, and notes but rejects the masculine reading that would make it the priest. Clarke reads it as property: whatever was laid on the altar became the Lord's and had to be wholly devoted. Ellicott turns the grammar round and makes it a prohibition — 'must be holy', nothing unholy may touch it, the future carrying imperative force as in the Ten Commandments.

Three passages in this catena are unusually rich and worth knowing about. Clarke at v.22 relays Houbigant's conjecture that the waving and heaving of the offerings traced the figure of the cross, and is careful to present it as a conjecture he will not assert. Clarke at v.30 turns the seven days into a full excursus on the number seven — the Hebrew number of perfection, the Essene formula preserved by Philo and Josephus, the Pythagorean triangle and square, Cicero's 'knot and cement of all things' — and ends by leaving the ancient philosophers to judge their own meaning. Calvin at v.38 refuses to let the oil and wine of the daily offering be read as flavouring, since God was not gratified by their savour and did not wish to make epicures of the priests under colour of religion.

Zero ENTITIES signals again, as in Exodus 26 — these tabernacle and consecration chapters carry almost no place-names. But two entries first graded B on repetition (2-3 and 19-21, ttr 0.562 and 0.579, dupfrac 0.000). The cause is the same as in Leviticus 7: the chapter's own vocabulary — bread, cake, unleavened, oil, blood, hands — recurs unavoidably. Fixed by varying the surrounding prose rather than cutting substance, which took both to A.

Clarke's table as scraped is internally corrupt: it prints 22,300 Levites in all with '3,580 fit for service and 13,720 unfit', where 8,580 + 13,720 = 22,300. I reported the two figures that add (22,300 total, 13,720 unfit) and left the garbled one alone. The live disagreement is real and worth keeping: Clarke's addition of the two censuses gives 22,300, while Keil and Ellicott both put the tribe at 22,000.

Ellicott and Wesley read the Gershonite load in opposite orders. Ellicott makes the first item the fine twined linen curtains of the mishkan (holding the woodwork subsidiary to them) and the goats' hair the tent's; Wesley makes the first item the goats' hair covering and the second the ten linen curtains. Kept as a debate rather than smoothed — the two readings assign the same objects to different phrases.

The catena for this chapter has no keys 10, 11 or 39, so pericope spans cannot be drawn freely: coverage_problems fails any entry covering a verse absent from the source. Spans therefore break at 9|12 (entry '3' runs 3-9, the next starts at 12) and the chapter's last entry stops at 38 rather than 39. Tiling verified at 36 keys.

JFB is residue everywhere in this chapter. Every JFB block is Exodus 26-27 material — the boards that formed the walls, the five cross bars and the middle bar, the dimensions of the brazen altar and its horns, the court's sixty brazen pillars — filed under Exodus 40 verses. Declared in excluded_voices on every entry whose span contains one.

Keil and Delitzsch appear at v2 and again at v35 as bare scripture text with no comment attached: the block quotes Exodus 40:2-9 and 40:35-38 verbatim and stops. Declared in excluded_voices on both entries rather than cited. Keil's substantive notes in this chapter sit at vv.18, 21, 23 and 30, and are used there.

The span ghost check caught a real misattribution. My first draft of the v2 entry credited Henry, alongside Wesley, with the computation that the first day of the first month fell fourteen days short of a year from the exodus. Henry's block is filed at v1, not v2; only Wesley carries that material within the span. Rewritten to Wesley alone, whose v2 note also supplies the Hezekiah precedent and the observation about the new moon — both of which the first draft had dropped.

Entries '1' and '27' first graded B on lexical variety (ttr 0.548 and 0.545) with dupfrac 0.000, no repeated n-grams and no duplicate sentences — nothing a reader would call repetition. The cause was density of function words in long 'the X of the Y' chains plus the chapter's own unavoidable nouns (tabernacle, altar, door, place, hanging). Both were rewritten with more varied diction and shorter genitive chains rather than cut for length, taking ttr to 0.705 and 0.692 and the chapter to 100 percent grade A.

Three readings of the tent spread abroad over the tabernacle, kept as a debate rather than smoothed. Gill takes it for the goats'-hair curtains; Clarke for the whole set of coverings of rams' skins and goats' hair thrown over the building, the tabernacle having no other roof; Ellicott separates the verse's two clauses, making the goats' hair the ohel proper and the rams' and seals' skins the miksêh laid above it.

Calvin denies the premise the chronological notes rest on. He cannot approve the opinion that the tabernacle was only now set up: it was complete before Moses' second ascent, and had stood pitched outside the camp in token of divorce since the golden calf, so the setting-up means its restoration to its proper place in the midst of the people. Clarke and Ellicott both reckon the dates on the opposite assumption. Recorded as a debate on the '2' entry.

JFB is residue in this chapter as elsewhere, and Keil's blocks at vv.2, 14 and 23 are bare scripture quotation with no comment attached — the text of the following verses reprinted and nothing more. Both declared in excluded_voices rather than cited. Keil is also excluded at the 30-32 entry, but for a different reason worth distinguishing: his block there quotes vv.30-33 and then comments on v.33, which falls outside that entry's span, so nothing in it is usable where it sits.

Two scrape defects in this chapter. Calvin's block at v.14 ends with an enormous scripture-index dump — several hundred bare references running from Genesis through the Psalms — appended after his comment on the four standards; it is StudyLight page furniture, not text. Gill's block at v.29 is a bare lemma, 'And Moses said unto Hobab, the son of Raguel the Midianite,' with no exposition following, so Gill is declared excluded on the Hobab entry.

Clarke came up excludable at two entries on the first ghost pass, and in both cases the fault was mine rather than the source's. His v.2 note (why two instruments could reach so vast an army, the pair differing in length and pitch, Josephus reserving one for the nobles) and his v.14 note (the whole marching order as a bare table) are real content that I had simply not used. Both were written in rather than excluded — excluded_voices is for residue, not for a writer's omissions.

The sound of the teruah is disputed three ways and cannot be harmonised. Gill hears a broken, uneven, quavering note and reaches for the onomatopoeia tara-tan-tara; Clarke agrees on the roughness and derives it from the Roman taratantara; Ellicott holds the exact opposite, that teruah is a loud unbroken blast distinguished from the convocation signal precisely by its continuity; Keil and Delitzsch relocate the contrast into the verbs, making one short sharp bursts and the other a sustained peal. Kept as a debate.

Calvin and Gill contradict each other outright on the three days' journey. Calvin reads a continuous three-day march, arguing that no tents were pitched until Paran and the people slept in the open air; Gill separates the stages, placing a month at Taberah and seven days at Hazeroth between them, and sets Bunting's eight miles from Sinai against the Targum of Jonathan's thirty-six. Both recorded; the entry does not adjudicate.

Calvin reverses the usual sense of 'thou mayest be to us instead of eyes' and says so explicitly, complaining that commentators do not appear to have observed the construction. Where Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott read the clause prospectively — Hobab is wanted for desert knowledge the cloud does not supply — Calvin insists the Hebrew carries more than one causal particle, making it retrospective: Hobab has already served as eyes and borne the inconveniences, and would forfeit his recompense by leaving now.

Drafting for lexical variety from the outset — short genitive chains, concrete nouns, varied verbs — held every entry in this chapter at grade A with no repetition-repair pass, where Exodus 40 needed two entries rewritten after they graded B on ttr alone. The remaining cost is still the ceiling: most first drafts landed 40 to 170 words over 650. The 21-28 entry ran the other way and had to be grown from 300 to 390, since that span is almost entirely 'See Gill on' stubs with only Gill at vv.21, 25 and 28, Wesley at v.21 and Ellicott at v.28 carrying content.

It is also one of the chapters the quality audit names as known-degenerate (ttr 0.31-0.37 alongside Joshua 17), and the reason is visible in the source: vv.19-36 are mostly one-line Clarke entries saying a place is unknown, with Gill supplying mileages and nothing else. Wide spans (16-25, 28-40, 41-49) were the only way to reach the floor without padding, and the middle entries are built almost entirely from Clarke's site identifications and Gill's distances.

JFB is residue throughout as usual. Two further exclusions are of a different kind: Keil's blocks at v.17 and v.55 are bare scripture quotation with no comment (declared excluded on the 16-25 and 55-56 entries), and Ellicott at v.40 is a single cross-reference, 'See Numbers 21:1, and Note' (excluded on 28-40). Verse 56 additionally carries the StudyLight CSS and nav-menu chrome after Ellicott's note, and Calvin's block at v.14 of the neighbouring chapter has the same defect.

Three ENTITIES signals, all of them my own tidying of the source rather than anything the sources said. I had written Elanitic where the scrape has Elantic, Moserah where Gill has Mosera, and Idumean where Clarke has 'a place in Idumea'. All three reverted to the source forms — including the apparent typo Elantic, on the Deuteronomy 2 precedent of keeping a source's orthography rather than silently correcting it. The general lesson is the same one the Numbers 10 note recorded: adjectives and normalised spellings I supply are attributions the catena does not carry.

A third word-count in the pipeline, worth knowing about. Entry 41-49 measured 647 by synthesis_qa.visible (which is what validate-synthesis uses and what the finish validator gates on) but 651 by audit-synthesis-quality's own tokeniser, which put it in the 651+ length bucket. My regex spot-check gave 639. Three counters, three answers; drafting to about 640 by QA.visible keeps clear of all of them.

Why Taberah is missing from the itinerary. Gill gives two answers — either it was the same place as Kibroth-hattaavah or lay beside it, or, on Aben Ezra's view, Israel camped there only one day and so it does not rank among the journeys. Clarke reasons from distance instead: three days' march were needed to reach this point, so other stations must have stood between and gone unrecorded because they were unremarkable. The two explanations are not compatible, since Clarke's makes the list selective and Gill's makes it complete.

Where Aaron died. Deuteronomy has Israel reaching Mosera from Bene-jaakan and places Aaron's death there; this chapter reverses the order and puts the death at Hor. Gill follows Jarchi in supposing they doubled back (Hashmonah to Mosera, then Bene-jaakan, then Mosera again, the two places twenty-four miles apart); Clarke resolves it geographically, making Mosera, Moseroth and Hor three names for one site, or Moseroth a village near the mountain. Recorded as a debate rather than harmonised.

Whether the gods of Egypt were literally overthrown. Wesley takes the clause doubly — the false gods were the beasts the Egyptians worshipped, which died when the firstborn of man and beast were struck, and their images too were probably thrown down as Dagon was before the ark. Calvin calls it a silly imagination that every idol toppled of itself, holding that God triumphed over them by proving they could not help their worshippers and by exposing the magicians' trickery.
